title: On-Call Drill
description: A paging incident, run by the book

domains.name: Detection
domains.description: The shared setup for this section, stated once: it is 03:10 on a Saturday. `checkout-api` is paging on a 5-minute burn-rate alert against a 99.9% availability SLO. The dashboard shows p99 latency flat, error rate at 4%, and a deploy that finished 20 minutes ago.

domains.name: Triage
domains.description: Same incident, twelve minutes in. The 4% errors are all HTTP 503 from one of six pods, which is `CrashLoopBackOff` with `OOMKilled` in its last state. Traffic is unchanged from last Saturday.

domains.name: Communication
domains.description: The incident is mitigated and you are writing it up. Two other teams consume `checkout-api`, and one customer opened a ticket during the window.

questions.prompt: What does a **burn-rate** alert tell you that a plain threshold alert does not?
options: That the service is down right now
How fast the error budget is being consumed relative to the window
Which pod is unhealthy
That a deploy happened recently
questions.explanation: Burn rate is error budget spend per unit time. A 4% error rate is fine for a 99% SLO and an emergency for a 99.99% one — the rate is what makes it actionable

questions.prompt: p99 latency is flat while errors are at 4%. What does that combination most likely rule out?
options: A bad deploy
Saturation — a resource-exhaustion slowdown affecting every request
A dependency outage
A configuration error
questions.explanation: Saturation almost always shows up as latency first. Flat latency with fast failures points at something rejecting requests outright, not something slowing them down

questions.prompt: Which of these are worth checking in the first two minutes?
options: The deploy that finished 20 minutes ago
Whether the error rate is uniform across pods
The quarterly capacity plan
Recent config or feature-flag changes
questions.explanation: Recent changes and the shape of the failure are cheap to check and narrow the search fast. Capacity planning is a Monday problem

questions.prompt: An alert that pages a human should always correspond to something a human can act on right now.
questions.explanation: An alert nobody can act on trains people to ignore alerts — which is how the actionable one gets missed

questions.prompt:
A pod is in `CrashLoopBackOff` with `OOMKilled` as its last state. What happened?

```
Last State: Terminated
  Reason:   OOMKilled
  Exit Code: 137
```
options: The liveness probe failed and the kubelet restarted it
The container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
The node ran out of disk and evicted it
The image failed to pull
questions.explanation: Exit 137 is SIGKILL (128 + 9). With `OOMKilled`, the container went over its memory limit — a probe failure would show a different reason

questions.prompt: Only one of six pods is affected, and traffic is unchanged. What does that most suggest?
options: A global memory leak that would eventually hit every pod
Something local to that pod or its node — a hot shard, a stuck request, a bad neighbour
An upstream dependency outage
A DNS failure
questions.explanation: A global cause would show up across the fleet. One pod out of six, at steady traffic, points somewhere local — though a slow leak that pod hit first is worth ruling out after mitigation

questions.prompt: Which actions mitigate **now**, before the cause is known?
options: Roll back the 20-minute-old deploy
Raise the memory limit and let it restart
Open a ticket for the memory profiling work
Take the pod out of rotation
questions.explanation: Mitigation restores service; diagnosis can wait for daylight. The ticket is the right instinct at the wrong moment

questions.prompt: Type the `kubectl` subcommand that shows a pod's recent events and its last termination state.
questions.explanation: `kubectl describe pod <name>` prints the event log and Last State — where `OOMKilled` and the exit code live

questions.prompt: Rolling back is an admission that the deploy was the cause.
questions.explanation: A rollback is a hypothesis test you can afford during an incident. If it does not help, you have ruled something out cheaply

questions.prompt: What belongs in the first status update, ten minutes in?
options: The root cause
What is broken, who is affected, what you are doing, and when you will update again
An apology and a timeline for the fix
Nothing until the incident is resolved
questions.explanation: Impact and the next update time are what readers need. A root cause guessed at ten minutes is usually wrong and gets quoted anyway

questions.prompt: Which postmortem finding is most likely to prevent a repeat?
options: "An engineer set the memory limit too low"
"Nothing catches a limit that is below the observed working set before it reaches production"
"We need to be more careful with limits"
"The alert fired too late"
questions.explanation: A finding that names a missing check produces work someone can do. Naming a person, or asking for more care, produces nothing

questions.prompt: The customer ticket arrived during the window. Which follow-ups are yours?
options: Confirm whether their failed requests fall inside the incident window
Close it as duplicate without checking
Link the ticket to the incident record
Tell them the root cause before it is established
questions.explanation: Match their symptoms against the window and link the record. A cause offered early is a correction owed later
